title: What you leave
hook: one Stoic idea that doesn't fit you

segments.voice: Yesterday: what you keep, askēsis, three habits out on the counter. Your line was my three. Did you write them down somewhere you'll see them? Day six hundred eighty-eight.

A friend lends you a cookbook from their grandmother's kitchen. You love it. You make the bread every Sunday now. But there's a chapter on organ meats that you read once, out of respect, and quietly decided was not for you. You didn't throw the book away. You didn't write an angry letter to the grandmother. You just left that chapter where it was. A year of Stoic reading can leave a chapter like that: an idea admired, or tried, or argued with, and finally set down. Today: what you leave.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER'S COOKBOOK.` → `BREAD EVERY SUNDAY.` → `ONE CHAPTER, LEFT WHERE IT IS.`

segments.voice: First, permission from Seneca himself. He was a committed Stoic, and still he wrote that he hadn't bound himself to any one master or borne anyone's name. In another letter he says the great thinkers who came before us are not our masters but our guides. And he quoted Epicurus, a rival, again and again, taking what was good wherever he found it. Leaving something behind is, oddly, a very Senecan thing to do. Second, some candidates. Some readers find a few Stoic ideas hard to live with. The hope of being entirely free of passions, which can sound like numbness. The claim that health, wealth, even the people we love, are indifferent to our true good. The old Stoic paradox that all wrongdoing is equally wrong. Epictetus's hardest words about grief. None of these is a misreading; they really are in the texts. And serious Stoics, then and now, have argued about them too. Third, how to leave well. Not with contempt. Name the idea fairly, in its strongest form, the way the Stoics would have stated it. Then say plainly, without a fight: not for me. You may come back to it in ten years and find it fits. Or not. Fourth, why this matters. Seneca read his teachers this way, as guides, keeping some things and leaving others, and the Stoic school itself kept arguing with its founders. Walking a philosophy as yourself is part of the tradition, not a break from it. The porch was always open on the sides. You can step off it, and step back on.
screen: `NOT OUR MASTERS, BUT OUR GUIDES.` · `SOME IDEAS ARE HARD TO LIVE WITH.` · `NAME IT FAIRLY, THEN SET IT DOWN.` · `WALK THE PATH AS YOURSELF.` · then, large: `NOT FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Think back over the year for one Stoic idea that never sat right with you. Let it come into view. Now state it, silently, in its strongest and fairest form, the way a good Stoic would. Notice that you can understand it and still not take it on. Then, gently, set it down, the way you'd close a chapter in a borrowed book. Say to yourself: not for me, at least not now. Notice what that leaves. The bell holds the time.
Epicurus, the rival philosopher Seneca kept quoting, taking what was good from any teacher, since the old thinkers are guides, not masters. Today's word.
Your line: not for me. Next to your three habits, write the one idea you're leaving, and one sentence on why, kindly. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

screen: `DAY 688 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A YEAR ON THE PORCH.`

howItsDone: Some modern readers of the Stoics adopt some of their practices while openly setting aside others, such as the ideal of being free of all passions or the paradox that all wrongs are equal.

fork.setup: you've found a Stoic idea that doesn't fit you. what would Seneca's example suggest?
options: name it fairly and set it down, keeping the rest
fork.reveal: Seneca called earlier thinkers guides, not masters, and borrowed from rivals; choosing is part of the path.

original.script: non domini nostri sed duces sunt
original.say: nohn DOH-mee-nee NOS-tree sed DOO-kays soont
original.note: Latin, Seneca's Letters 33: they are not our masters but our guides.

trapdoor: what you thought: studying a philosophy means taking all of it or none.
what it means: you can keep what fits and leave, fairly and kindly, what doesn't.
what a scholar hears: Letters 33.11, non domini nostri sed duces sunt; Letters 45.4, Seneca bound to no master; Cicero's Stoic Paradoxes 3 on all wrongs being equal.

notes: Letters 33.11 (non domini nostri sed duces sunt) and 45.4 (non enim me cuiquam emancipavi, nullius nomen fero) paraphrased. Confirm Latin and references.
Seneca quoting Epicurus: Letters 2–29 regularly close with an Epicurean maxim (see day 654).
Stoic paradox that all wrongs are equal: Cicero, Paradoxa Stoicorum 3; Diogenes Laërtius 7.120. Confirm.
Candidates for 'leaving' are presented as ones many readers struggle with, not as errors.

Review (y2 editor, days 670–688): cut 'a path you can only take whole is a path that's using you' (reads as a judgment on paths that ask for whole commitment); review fixed to match day 687's rewritten counter image; hook's 'after a year on the porch' (echoing 686) and its telling the listener reworded; 'many readers' softened; practice no longer tells the listener what they feel.
